title: Difficult parents
hookLine: a father hurt and embarrassed in the street; a son with a bowl who stays kind and doesn't stop
tomorrow: what do two partners owe each other?

cards: Three texts in an hour: where are you, who's there, why aren't you answering? Love, arriving as pressure. So what about when a parent is hard to be around?
The tradition tells a story about the Buddha's own father, a king, standing in the street, hurt and embarrassed, because his son was walking past the houses with a begging bowl.

teach.b: Tradition says that when the Buddha came home to Kapilavatthu, he walked the city with his bowl, house to house, the way monks gather food. His father, King Suddhodana, heard and rushed out. Why do you shame me?
No one in our family has ever begged. Picture the sting on both sides: a father who wanted a prince, a son who had become something else. The Buddha didn't put the bowl away to keep the peace.
And he didn't scold his father, or walk off.
He said, gently: this is the custom of my lineage. Not the royal line. The line of Buddhas.
Then, the story says, he spoke verses about living well, and the king was moved. Kind, and clear, at once. Two qualities from the teaching sit underneath that.
Karuna, compassion: feeling the other's hurt, and wishing it less. And upekkha, equanimity: steady enough not to be pushed off your own ground. Compassion without steadiness gives in.
Together, a boundary can be warm.

One more thing, plainly: if a parent ever makes home unsafe, kindness doesn't mean staying in harm's way. Reach out to someone you trust, or to local emergency help; in the US, you can call or text 988.

how: Some Buddhist teachers pair compassion (karuna) with equanimity (upekkha) when lay students ask about hard family relationships; the four brahmaviharas are practiced together, not one alone.

o: parents who must be cut off for your own practice
parents whose bad karma their children inherit
parents met with warmth and a steady boundary

games.q: a son, a father, a bowl — tap the pairs.
p: feeling the hurt, wishing it less

s: in the story, the Buddha put his bowl away to keep the peace with his father
tradition says he kept walking for alms, and answered gently: this is the custom of my lineage.
compassion and equanimity are taught as partners, not opposites
compassion without steadiness gives in; steadiness without compassion goes cold.
honoring parents in Buddhism means staying even when home is unsafe
kindness doesn't mean staying in harm's way; reach out to someone you trust or emergency help.

games.q: you're the son with the bowl. your father, the king, is in the street, hurt and embarrassed. what do you do?
o: go home with him and stop the alms round, to spare his feelings.
tell him firmly he's attached to pride and walk on.
keep the bowl, and tell him gently what it means to you.
games.why: tradition says the Buddha kept to his alms round and answered kindly: this is the custom of my lineage, the line of Buddhas. kind and clear at once.

practice: Rest one hand on your chest and feel its warmth: that's the kind part. Press both feet flat on the floor and feel how steady they are: that's the clear part. Breathe with both at once, warm and steady.
If a hard face or a hard text comes to mind, keep the hand where it is and the feet where they are, and let it be met by both for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Difficult parents: met with karuna and upekkha together, warm and steady. A boundary that doesn't stop being kind, like a son who keeps his bowl and still answers his father gently.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: compassion, feeling another's pain and wishing it eased.

carryVoice: For the pocket: kind and clear, a warm hand on the chest and steady feet on the floor. Three of eleven, on family.

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary on verses 168-169, and the Jataka introduction (Nidanakatha): the Buddha's alms round in Kapilavatthu, Suddhodana's protest, 'this is the custom of my lineage'
Dhammapada 168-169 (verses on living the good life, spoken to Suddhodana according to the commentary)
Digha Nikaya 13 and elsewhere (the four brahmaviharas, including karuna and upekkha)
